view: A report says reciting the sura's beginning and end gives light from head to foot, while reciting all of it gives light from earth to heaven.
The sura's opening follows the previous sura's affirmation of true revelation and humility: praise for an upright warning Quran that rebukes claims of a divine son and promises believers reward.
Idh can depend on an omitted 'remember,' introducing the remembered flight; it cannot attach to the preceding question or ḥasibt because the Prophet's perception was long after their retreat.
Other parses attach idh to ʿajaban or kānū in the previous verse, linking this scene to that clause.
note: The omitted 'remember' parse is also reported by these sources.

view: Eliding the hamza after the dhāl of idh makes the liaison smooth without changing meaning.
Awā means to go, return, settle, or take refuge; they made the cave their dwelling and shelter. Maʾwā is a place of return or refuge.
Fitya denotes young men, but fatā may also denote a fully grown man. It can figuratively name rulers even when old and may admit the sense of a servant.
note: Bursevi cites a prophetic preference for 'my young man' over 'my slave'; Abu Yusuf allows the latter sense.

view: Raqīm is understood as a book, a stone tablet recording the youths' story at the cave, or more generally something written or inscribed.
note: Ibn Kathir prefers the written or inscribed sense and compares the patterns qatil and jarih.

view: Fitya is a plural or collective form of fatā, analogous to ghilma and ṣibya; this formation is not freely productive.
note: Some call it a broken plural of paucity; Ibn al-Sarrāj and others call it a collective noun.

view: Naming the youths explicitly instead of using a pronoun highlights their youth, close ages, courage, judgment, steadfastness, and defense of truth; alternatively, ownership of the cave is established only after their retreat.
One report makes the youths eight and names Maksalmina as the eldest spokesman, with seven others; another describes seven secret worshippers joined by a shepherd.
note: The reported counts differ.

view: The foreign names have weak transmission; al-Tabari's list includes Makselminya, Majseliniya, Tamlikha, Martus, Kashutunus, Birunus, Dinamus, and Yatūnus, with Yemlikha sent to town.
The youths are described as freeborn, richly dressed Roman nobles or princes, from prominent families; some reports instead call them scholars, bathhouse workers, or royal ministers.
note: Reports mention gold ornaments and sidelocks.

view: Mujahid says at least one youth was so young that he had only a downy beard.
Accounts place them under the pagan Roman ruler Decius or Daqyanus in Ephesus, as followers of Jesus preserving monotheism amid persecution and idol worship.
note: The ruler's name has variants; Decius may underlie its Arabic form.

view: A competing account puts the youths before Jesus; Ibn Qutayba says Jesus later disclosed their story and they were raised between Jesus and Muhammad.
note: Other accounts make them Jesus' followers.

view: A reported alternative calls Daqyanus a Magian or Zoroastrian who promoted that religion.
note: Competes with the pagan Roman account.

view: A detailed account says Decius tortured believers, pressed the eight youths to worship idols, and brought them before him after informers found them praying for deliverance.
note: The youths refused; one version says victims were displayed on city walls.

view: The king stripped the youths of rank and jewelry and delayed punishment, sending them home to reconsider; they resolved to flee before his return.
Another account says the youths were noble festival-goers who independently received faith, cautiously disclosed their shared belief in pairs, then withdrew to a cave.
note: One version places their meeting under a tree, another outside the city; a hunting dog accompanied them.

view: One escape account has them disguise their movement toward the cave with a polo mallet and ball; another has them slip away while playing at a public festival.
note: A further version says they feigned hunting.

view: Another explanation says they fled the ruler because one youth was accused of a crime.
Wahb's account has a disciple of Jesus convert noble youths while working at a bathhouse; blamed for the deaths of the king's son and a woman, they flee with a farmer and dog.
note: The king later sealed them in the cave.

view: One youth proposed his father's cave; after the group entered, their people sealed it, and a later Christian king removed the barrier, leading to their awakening.
note: They then guessed they had slept a day or part of one; the king expected hunger and thirst to kill them.

view: Fearing the king's return, each youth took money from his father's house, gave some away, and left with the dog for a mountain cave.
Inside the cave they worshiped, prayed, praised God, and entrusted Yemliha with buying food and gathering news while disguised as a poor man.
When Decius returned and ordered sacrifices, Yemliha learned the youths were sought, warned them, and they prostrated, prayed for protection, and ate his small evening meal.
Decius searched for the missing youths, said he would have forgiven repentance, and was urged by nobles to question and punish their parents.
Two secret believers, Bedros and Ronas, recorded the youths' names, ancestry, and story on lead tablets in a sealed copper chest near the cave for future believers.
note: Other versions say lead or copper tablets were hidden at home or in the king's construction.

view: The youths' people searched but could not find the cave; later generations recorded their names, and a Muslim king followed the earlier ruler.
One account says the youths slept in the cave for 309 years.
Accounts differ whether their dog was a youth's hunting dog, the shepherd's dog, or belonged to Maksalmina, a sheep-owner; names include Himran and Qitmir.
A report says Daqyanus imposed idol worship in Ephesus or Tarsus, seven secret worshippers fled with a shepherd and dog, and God blinded pursuers who then sealed the cave.
Another report says the youths learned faith from a disciple or earlier believers, rejected the king's idols, and answered his summons with declarations resembling verses 14–16.
The reports disagree over whether the ruler discovered their faith before or after escape, whether they planned together or met by chance, and whether a shepherd or only his dog joined.
Quraysh consulted Jewish scholars about the youths, a world-traveling man, and the spirit as questions to test Muhammad's prophethood.
A second report says Jewish scholars judged that answering all three questions would disprove prophethood, while answering two and withholding one would confirm it.
Another report says Quraysh sent three men to Jewish scholars in Najran to ask about the cave youths, Moses' companion, Dhul-Qarnayn, and the Hour.
note: This differs from the three-question report.

view: Long-sleep-and-awakening stories are also reported in Indian scriptures, the Talmud, and the Christian Seven Sleepers tradition.
note: The Talmudic examples span 70 or 60 years.

view: Most historians place the episode between Jesus and Muhammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though Christians preserved it extensively and some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews.
Christian accounts resemble Ibn Ishaq's report in some respects but differ over the sleepers' number, their dog, and the length of sleep.
The cave story circulated in detailed transmissions attributed to al-Qummi, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq, Wahb, al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, and others.
Transmitted accounts diverge on major features and still more on dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title Companions of al-Raqim.
One explanation for divergent reports is the story's prominence among People of the Book and the spread of Christian images and monuments, which let communities reshape it.
Another explanation is broad Muslim collection of outside accounts through converts such as Wahb and Kaʿb, with later transmitters treating such material as prophetic reports.
Ibn Abbas is reported to say he knew the Quran except the meanings of ḥannān, awwāh, and raqīm, and was unsure whether raqīm was a book or a building.
Andalusian usage called Christians Rūm rather than Naṣārā.
The youths asked for persecution to be lifted while declaring God alone Lord of heaven and earth and rejecting any other deity as outrageous falsehood.
The believing youths fled their persecuting, unbelieving people and took refuge in the cave to preserve their religion.
Their small number and inexperience underscore that youth can be more receptive to truth and better guided than elders; awakened conviction made them disregard danger and expediency.

The Quran selects the narrative details that guide rather than giving a complete history; it omits names, ancestry, occupations, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog's identity, which later accounts supplied divergently.
note: Kuranyolu calls guesses about the number baseless speculation known only to God.

view: Their cave retreat for faith parallels Muhammad and Abu Bakr's retreat to the cave of Thawr.
The opening outline shows the youths' protection as support for faith, while the full narrative of flight, sleep, awakening, discovery, and public sign unfolds afterward.
note: The outline keeps the story's guiding purpose ahead of secondary detail.

view: The cave account illustrates resurrection and the coming Hour through the youths' prolonged sleep, awakening, and the townspeople's recognition.
God effaced their self-awareness in witnessing unity and divine self-sufficiency, then restored sober discrimination after union.
Spiritually the youths are people of gnosis whose chivalry abandons everything besides God for solitude with Him; their communion drives further ascent through blissful stations.
Seen from one's own human perspective, the youths provoke flight; viewed from the Real, one perceives divine unity and lordship in them and stands firm.
note: Jaʿfar compares the Prophet's flight from unbelievers to the human perspective.

view: Viewing created beings from one's own position turns sight away from the youths; the Prophet both beholds God and is beheld from Him.
The youths' surrounding lights of the Real, exaltation, and awe explain why the Prophet would flee upon seeing them.
The Prophet would recoil from the youths' overwhelming spiritual states despite recognizing their lofty nearness and witnessing.
The unbearable awe of God's power, care, and guardianship in them means flight from them is truly flight from God.
Angelic lights honor, while human lights guide outwardly and inwardly; their greater awe is compared with Satan fleeing ʿUmar.
Their long life can symbolize remembrance that carries a person beyond ordinary time.
Kahf denotes a large, wide mountain cave; the Companions of the Cave are those said to have slept there for years and awakened.
The cave is identified as Khayram in Mount Yanjalus or Banjulus.
A reported saying values believers who mingle with people and patiently endure harm over those who avoid people and their harm.
note: This bears on whether retreat or social participation is preferable.

view: Reports call believers' homes their cloisters and say some veterans of Badr stayed home after ʿUthman's killing until their burial.
note: The cloister saying is described as mursal from al-Hasan and others.

view: The Prophet reportedly advised ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir to hold his tongue, remain at home, and weep over his sin as a path to salvation.
A Bukhari report describes a time when a Muslim's best possession will be sheep taken to mountain heights and rain-fed places to flee fitna for faith.
A report attributed to the Prophet permits celibacy, seclusion, and mountain retreat for the community in year 180 AH.
A report says that in a corrupt age only flight from peak to peak or stone to stone preserves religion, and family demands for unaffordable provision can ruin a person.
Wahb warned a would-be recluse that people need one another and advised hearing without listening, seeing without looking, and speaking little.
A report says God admires a shepherd who prays alone on a mountain crag from fear of Him, forgives him, and admits him to Paradise.
The cave at Rujayb in Jordan is considered the strongest archaeological and reported fit after centuries as a forgotten ruin, though no proposal is identified conclusively.
Other proposed caves lie on Mount Qasiyun near Damascus, at Petra, in Scandinavia, and near Nakhchivan; the latter two conflict with the Roman setting and reach of Roman power.
Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a prominent city that remained under Roman rule from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.
God preserved the youths during their long sleep through the cave's position and His care; their steadfastness and revival became a public sign.
The youths' flight establishes leaving family, homeland, wealth, and friends to preserve religion under persecution; the Prophet and Companions likewise emigrated.
Retreat into mountains, caves, or other solitude is a practice of prophets and saints, especially amid corruption and fitna.
note: Mosque retreat, coast, frontier, or home can serve the same purpose.

view: Seclusion can occur on mountains, at coasts and frontiers, or at home; during fitna, hiding and guarding one's tongue is advised.
One view makes seclusion separation from evil while remaining among people, inwardly and in conduct.
Ibn al-Mubarak describes seclusion as joining others in God's remembrance and keeping silent when they speak of other matters.
Capacities differ: cave retreat is the highest state, home seclusion suits others, and some can mix outwardly while inwardly distinct.
The cave is the body; entering bodily existence and using its faculties can develop intellectual and practical perfection on a steady course toward God.
note: Mercy comes from the beautiful divine names according to one's readiness.

view: The cave symbolizes the heart as a place of withdrawal after despairing of the world's kindness and seeking God's protection alone.
Outwardly the cave sheltered them; inwardly divine care took charge of them and brought spiritual states while they were absent from themselves.
The youths' flight can signify seekers' retreat from the self and the darkness of existence toward encounter with divine beauty and majesty.
The fāʾ indicates that they hurried to pray immediately upon reaching the cave.
The mercy sought is provision from God, and 'from Your presence' means from Him.

words: رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةًۭ وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًۭا
view: A transmitted supplication asks God to make every affair's outcome good and protect from worldly disgrace and punishment in the afterlife.
They turned to supplication after fleeing their pursuers; their prayer for guidance and perseverance was fitting at this precarious moment.

words: رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةًۭ وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًۭا
view: The prayer can concern worldly needs and an exit from their situation, while they trust their afterlife outcome; mercy may also encompass the afterlife.
note: Al-Alusi rejects restricting it to worldly affairs and takes it as a prayer for both worlds.

words: رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةًۭ وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًۭا
view: The prayer asks comprehensively for mercy, good, right guidance, and deliverance in this world and the next, which God grants beyond expectation.

words: رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةًۭ وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًۭا
view: The verse is recommended as a sufficient prayer for a believer's worldly affairs.
Against attributing the later certain promise of mercy and provision to the youths, Islahi calls it God's speech: a humble person could voice such assurance only as prayer or yearning, as here.
Their prayer disavows their own power and sincerely turns to God, who answers, relieves their need, and gives them refuge.
The expression can imply an omitted noun, 'a thing of right guidance,' then an omitted enabling object: prepare what lets us attain guidance.
Both prepositional phrases attach to 'prepare.'
'From Your presence' presents the mercy as great, special, abundant, and directly associated with God's own generous stores, beyond common mercy.
note: Bursevi says these hidden treasuries are inaccessible to hostile eyes.

view: Their direct appeal to God after reaching the cave expresses exhausted worldly means and desperate need for divine support.
Their affair is their escape from unbelievers and continuing obedience; they request a guided path to safety and deliverance.
note: Tabatabai stresses that persecutors killed believers and forced idolatry.

view: They ask God to make their entire affair itself rightly guided or rightly ordered, not only to show them a guided path.
note: Al-Zamakhshari likens the expression to calling someone a lion.

view: The expression recognizes mercy as God's gratuitous gift, not something He owes them.
The requested mercy includes forgiveness and provision.
The mercy is guidance in religion rather than, or alongside, provision.
note: Baghawi presents guidance and provision as alternatives; Tabatabai mentions guidance as a gift reserved to God.

view: Mercy includes forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies; other explanations include guidance, knowledge, patience, and shelter from persecution.
note: Al-Alusi prefers an unrestricted mercy encompassing these examples and more.

view: They ask for divine mercy that saves them from unbelievers and persecution, conceals them from their people, and shelters them.
They ask God for mercy sufficient to make them independent of everyone else.

words: رَحْمَةًۭ وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًۭا
view: If mercy means divine support, the guidance request explains that support; if mercy means a particular divine gift, guidance is an additional request.

words: رَحْمَةًۭ وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًۭا
view: The later advice to enter the cave confidently anticipates mercy and ease, the very gifts requested in this prayer.
The paired mercy and knowledge given to Khiḍr echo the youths' prayer for mercy from God's presence.
Mercy is preservation in God's remembrance, or remembrance and gratitude in every state.
The highest hidden order of events is divinely bestowed beyond customary or extraordinary events; the youths seek that kind of mercy.
Hayyiʾ means set right, make ready, or make easy; its root means bringing a thing into a particular state or form.
The hamza of hayyiʾ is written on alif here; seating by the preceding vowel is more usual, but some Arabs use alif throughout, analogical to the hamza's origin.
Fronting the phrases gives prominence to the favor sought and states the petition's object early; the construction may extract right guidance from the affair to mean making the whole affair right.
Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, and al-Zuhri read the form with two yāʾs and no hamza, replacing a quiescent hamza.
A reading transmitted from al-Aʿshā through Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim omits the audible hamza; it may reflect replacement or deletion, with disputed analysis of the resulting weak letter.
note: Abu Hayyan calls replacement regular and permits deletion in imperative or jussive forms; al-Samin cites a poem for weak-letter retention.

view: Replacing the hamza with yāʾ may shift the root from h-y-ʾ to h-w-y, changing 'prepare' toward 'make desirable' or 'incline.'
The codex attributed to ʿAbd Allāh reportedly wrote words such as shayʾan and yastahziʾūn with alif where a different hamza seat is more common.
They ask God to facilitate their affair and guide them to a sound course or action that pleases Him and draws them near Him.
note: Tabari includes escape from disbelief and idolatry; Ibn Abbas is reported to seek deeds God loves.

view: Rushd is right guidance, correctness, soundness, or consciousness of what is right, opposite to error and directed toward a desired end.
note: Ibn Ashur says the ḍamma form is especially used for sound handling of property.

view: Abu Raja reads rushdan with ḍamma on rāʾ and silent shīn; the common reading rashadan has both vowels open, with the same general meaning.
The open-vowel rashadan is preferred because it matches the surrounding verse endings.
Among famous readings, this verse has only the open-vowel form; 2:256 and 4:6 have only ḍamma, while the 18:66 variants reflect nearby cadence.
note: At 18:66, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub use fatḥa; named other readers use ḍamma.

view: Right guidance is a safe way out of the cave.
Moses' request for sound judgment echoes the cave youths' request for sound judgment in their affairs.
